title: Unveiling the Mass Transfer and Particle Size Release Mechanisms of Polydisperse Colloidal Emulsions in Porous Media Under Low Hydraulic Conditions
content:
Abstract

Polydisperse colloids play a vital role in groundwater contaminant remediation and stabilization, fermentable substrate delivery, and active ingredient transport. Although significant progress has been made in the field of polydisperse colloids, which are mainly polydisperse colloidal suspensions, little is known about polydisperse colloidal emulsions, especially under low flow conditions (<0.1 m/d). Herein, a series of column experiments combined with dynamic light scattering were conducted to investigate the mass transfer and particle size release of polydisperse colloidal emulsions in porous media under low hydraulic conditions. The results demonstrated that a significant particle size separation effect between the released and retained colloids occurred in the polydisperse colloidal emulsion at low flow rates, which could not be explained by classical colloid filtration theory. This discrepancy was attributed to the differences in the polydisperse colloidal emulsion size release mechanism between high and low flow rates. Unlike the dominant role of hydraulic drag at >0.1 m/d, viscosity governs colloid release at <0.1 m/d. Notably, the viscosity decreased for polydisperse colloidal emulsions at a low flow rate during mass transfer rather than being constant, as traditionally assumed. Hence, the influence of viscosity on the polydisperse colloidal emulsion particle size release behavior at low flow rates cannot be ignored. In this situation, an optimized viscosity recurrence function was developed, which successfully reproduced the particle size distribution behavior across the full range of flow rates. These findings enhance predicting viscosity-governed polydisperse emulsion transport under low-flow rates, guiding particle fate, colloid-facilitated co-transport, and emulsion flooding.
